title: Shifted calling seasons gave no clear repeated prediction gain for two frog species in two US regions in 2001-2015
abstract: We tested whether a temperature shift improves calling predictions for wood frogs and green frogs in the US Northeast and Midwest. We fit 2001-2008 and 2009-2015 separately and left each year out in turn. We reused verified public panels from a prior SCI study. The 60 folds scored 13,938 species-survey records at 501 routes. Seven of eight Brier gains were positive, but only one conditional 95 percent year-block range was above zero. All wider ranges for eight comparisons crossed zero. Log-loss gains were positive in six tests. All shifted-model residual temperature slopes had ranges that crossed zero. Removing 2012 from evaluation reduced both late Midwest gains. The tests do not establish a general prediction gain or a lack of value. Short periods, shared training among folds, fixed seasonal shape and selected known route-observer groups limit inference. Window and route choices use the full source record. These are conditional weather hindcasts, not population forecasts or causal climate effects. Code, reusable input panels, scored predictions, source hashes, checks and a figure are included.

display.caption: Held-out-year Brier score gains and residual temperature slopes. Lines show conditional 95 percent year-block bootstrap ranges. Periods are fit separately. Positive gain favors the shifted model.

citations.reason: Reuse verified panels and model code. Extend the extreme-year test to every held-out year in separately fitted periods. Same underlying records; no independent data validation.
